What Are the Implications of Setting Aside More Revenue in “Boom” Years?
Prop. 2 would require the state to set aside more revenue in years when capital gains revenues spike. This change would allow the state to build up the rainy day fund and pay down certain debts faster, reducing future General Fund cost pressures, while modestly curtailing General Fund revenue available for immediate spending needs.
If Prop 2’s “excess” capital gains provisions had been in place between 2010-11 and 2023-24, California would have had to set aside more General Fund revenue in six of those 14 years. This additional set-aside would have amounted to less than 1% or 2% of total General Fund revenue in each of those six years. Capital gains revenue is difficult to project. However, if a similar pattern held going forward, Prop. 2 could take hundreds of millions of dollars — or even more than $1 billion — in revenue “off the table” in some years. This would reduce resources available to address urgent needs that arise, but would also help to pay down additional state debt and further build reserves to address future emergencies.
Although “excess” capital gains revenue, by definition, is not a predictable and reliable revenue source and cannot be counted on to fund ongoing services, it could be reasonable to use it to temporarily meet critical needs. For example, the state could provide more funding for food banks in the wake of federal food assistance cuts, boost support for local governments to address homelessness, and pay child care providers before or at the time of service delivery (rather than after) — a change that would increase providers’ financial solvency.
In certain years, Prop. 2 would modestly reduce revenue that could otherwise be used to support vital services as communities across the state are reeling from deep federal cuts and mounting affordability pressures that are compounding long-standing unmet needs.
However, meaningfully addressing Californians’ needs requires significant and sustained new revenue — well beyond the relatively modest revenue that Prop. 2 would occasionally divert to reserves and debt payments. This underscores the need to reform California’s outdated tax base whether or not voters approve Prop. 2.
What Are the Implications of Expanding the Types of Debt That May Be Paid Down with Set-Aside Revenues?
The state Constitution requires a portion of General Fund revenues to be set aside each year for certain debt payments (unfunded pension and state retiree health liabilities). This requirement cannot be reduced or suspended even in a budget emergency — a provision that Prop. 2 would leave in place. In recent years, for example, roughly $1 billion to $2 billion in General Fund revenues each year remained “off the table” and were not available to support urgent spending needs.
Prop. 2 would broaden the allowable uses of set-aside revenues to include unemployment insurance (UI) debt. If policymakers were to use these debt-paydown funds to repay the principal on the state’s federal UI loans, then a cost currently borne by businesses would be shifted to the state .
Prop. 2 would also allow set-aside revenues to be used to pay down certain obligations related to TK-14 education and Medi-Cal that otherwise would be paid out of the General Fund. If policymakers were to use debt-paydown funds for these purposes, then General Fund revenue would be freed up for other purposes .
However, set-aside revenues are limited. If state leaders were to use more of these debt-paydown funds for the new purposes allowed by Prop. 2, then fewer (or no) funds would be available to reduce unfunded pension and state retiree health liabilities — costs that would eventually be borne by the General Fund.
What Are the Implications of Using Set-Aside Revenues to Repay Unemployment Insurance Loans?
Prop. 2 would allow state leaders to use set-aside revenues for “federal loans made to the Unemployment Fund.” California owes the federal government roughly $20 billion it borrowed to cover the cost of workers’ unemployment insurance (UI) benefits beginning during the COVID-19 pandemic, when unemployment spiked. Using debt-paydown funds to reduce the principal on California’s UI debt would shift a cost currently borne by businesses to the state and do nothing to fix California’s broken UI system.
Shifting a Cost Currently Borne by Businesses to the State
California’s state government is not required to repay the principal on federal UI loans. Instead, federal law requires businesses to repay the principal through automatic increases in their federal payroll taxes. This makes sense: California’s UI debt is the result of a broken system (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/revitalizing-unemployment-insurance-in-california/). For decades, state leaders have not required businesses to contribute enough to cover the true cost of the unemployment benefits their workers need.
Using set-aside revenues to repay the principal on California’s UI loans would shift a cost currently covered by businesses to the state. Moreover, this approach would reduce the amount of debt-paydown funds available for other purposes, such as reducing unfunded pension liabilities — costs that would eventually be borne by the General Fund. As a result, to the extent that state leaders were to use set-aside revenues to pay down UI debt, then more General Fund revenue would be needed to reduce other state debts, diverting dollars away from providing services to Californians.
Doing Nothing to Fix California’s Broken UI System
The UI system is chronically underfunded (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/revitalizing-unemployment-insurance-in-california/) because California has failed to modernize the system’s financing to ensure that it generates sufficient revenue to cover the cost of the unemployment benefits workers need.
Consequently, federal loans are expected to become “a permanent feature (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4943)” of the program, with significant implications for the state’s budget. California typically uses General Fund dollars to pay the interest on these loans, which could total around $1 billion annually in the coming years. Using state dollars to pay the interest on UI loans reduces resources that could otherwise be used to address Californians’ affordability challenges or other needs.
Using debt-paydown funds to reduce the principal on California’s UI debt could modestly reduce the state’s annual interest payments in the near term. However, until state leaders address the broken UI financing system, California is expected to remain locked in a perpetual cycle of debt, necessitating ongoing federal loans and putting constant pressure on the state’s General Fund to cover the annual interest owed.
What Are the Implications of Using Set-Aside Revenues to Repay Certain School and Community College (TK-14) Education Obligations?
Prop. 2 would give state leaders a new option to use set-aside revenues to repay certain TK-14 education obligations. Specifically, the measure would allow state leaders to use these funds to 1) cover Prop. 98 “settle up” payments (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5110#Settle_Up), as needed, and 2) more quickly phase out an outstanding debt tied to an accounting maneuver that state leaders adopted in the 2023-24 budget (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4929) to address an issue related to the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. These new options mean that:
State Leaders Could Use Debt-Paydown Funds to Help Address Increases in Prop. 98 Funding Estimates
When state leaders enact a budget, they provide an estimate of the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee for that fiscal year. This initial estimate is updated in subsequent years to reflect changes in revenue estimates and other inputs. The updated inputs sometimes increase the Prop. 98 guarantee, which requires the state to provide additional funding through “settle-up” payments.
The state usually recognizes any increases to the Prop. 98 guarantee in subsequent years and provides the required settle-up payments from the state’s General Fund at that point. In some years, however, settle-up payments have been delayed, most recently for fiscal years 2024-25 and 2025-26, partly due to the state’s limited General Fund capacity to fund that growth.
Prop. 2 would allow set-aside revenues to be used to cover any current or future Prop. 98 settle-up obligations. This change would provide state leaders with an additional funding source for making these payments, which they could use at their discretion, potentially in combination with General Fund dollars. However, using debt-paydown funds for this purpose would compete with other allowable uses, such as prefunding state retiree health benefits.
In addition, using debt-paydown funds to make settle-up payments would not necessarily retire this obligation more quickly. Under current law, there is no required schedule for making settle-up payments, and Prop. 2 does not create one. If set-aside revenues were treated as the sole or primary source for settle-up payments, it could take longer to fully pay down these obligations because the amount of set-aside revenues may not align with the size of the obligation in a given year, especially when state revenues decline and the set-aside shrinks.
State Leaders Could Accelerate the State’s Recognition of $6.2 Billion in TK-14 Costs Incurred in 2022-23
In 2023, tax filing deadlines were extended due to winter storms, and state leaders overestimated the amount of tax revenue that would be received later in the year. As a result, the state provided $6.2 billion more to schools and community colleges than the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee actually required.
State leaders did not reduce the minimum guarantee to account for the lower revenues. Instead, they set up a schedule to recognize those dollars for accounting purposes in future budgets, starting in 2027-28 and ending in 2039-40. The annual cost is $500 million for the first 12 years, with a smaller amount in the 13th year.
Recognizing these costs will directly reduce General Fund revenues that would otherwise be available in those years for state funding priorities outside of the Prop. 98 guarantee. The sooner this $6.2 billion debt is recognized, the sooner the annual General Fund cost ends and those dollars become available for other purposes.
Prop. 2 would allow state leaders to use set-aside revenues to recognize this $6.2 billion debt, which would mitigate the General Fund impact as well as potentially clear the outstanding balance more quickly. However, using debt-paydown funds for this purpose would compete with other allowable uses, such as reducing state retiree pension liabilities.
What Are the Implications of Changing the Relationship Between Reserves and the State Spending Cap (Gann Limit)?
Prop. 2 would allow state policymakers to save more in strong revenue years to better protect vital public services during economic downturns. This is because deposits into two key reserves would no longer count as spending for the purpose of calculations required by California’s spending cap (the Gann Limit). Instead, these deposits would count toward the Gann Limit only when they are withdrawn .
This change would allow state leaders to build up reserves in years when revenues are strong and the state is close to reaching the spending cap, removing a key drawback of the Gann Limit. This change would also modestly increase “room” under the cap by up to a few billion dollars a year, potentially delaying how long it takes for the state to surpass the limit.
These changes are important. The Gann Limit is an arbitrary cap that hinders state leaders’ ability (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/) to respond to the needs of Californians, which have changed dramatically since late 1970s when the cap was established. Meeting the essential needs of residents and building up reserves to address future needs should not be hamstrung by an arbitrary spending cap approved by an earlier generation of voters.
Prop. 2 would allow policymakers to keep the state under the Gann Limit by making deposits into two reserves — the BSA and the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account (“holding account” (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-rainy-day-fund-and-other-budget-reserves-overview/)). Several factors, including which of these accounts were used for this purpose, would determine when the deposited funds could be withdrawn and how they could be spent. Specifically:
For deposits into the holding account , state law currently requires the funds to be withdrawn within a year — a rule that could be changed by the Legislature.
If withdrawing funds from the holding account would cause the state to exceed the spending cap, then policymakers would lose flexibility over how the funds could be used (their use would be governed by the Gann Limit’s restrictive rules (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/)).
Otherwise, if withdrawing the funds would not cause the state to exceed the limit, policymakers would have full control over the funds.
For deposits into the BSA , the portion that was constitutionally required to be deposited could not be withdrawn unless a budget emergency was operative. Any discretionary deposits, on the other hand, could be withdrawn at any time.
If withdrawing funds from the BSA would cause the state to exceed the spending limit, then policymakers would lose flexibility over how the funds could be used (their use would be governed by the Gann Limit’s restrictive rules (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/)).

Endorsement: Prop 2 could help California be more fiscally responsible — if our politicians bother to use it
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 15, 2026
Proposition 2 would help California stabilize its budget by requiring more money for its rainy-day reserve and setting aside more funding to pay off debts.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
What would you do if you suddenly found yourself flush with an unexpected cash windfall?
Would you run out and treat yourself to something expensive and irresponsible? Or would you pay off your debts and sock the extra money away for a rainy day?
Proposition 2 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop2-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which Democratic state lawmakers (and one Republican) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20) placed on California’s November ballot, would encourage California to take the latter approach with its budget.

Understanding how requires a bit of backstory.
California’s budget relies heavily on a progressive tax structure; 1% of the richest taxpayers account for 50% of the state’s income taxes (https://www.lao.ca.gov/LAOEconTax/Article/Detail/7).
But this structure is volatile. If the stock market takes a hit, so do California’s tax revenues and the critical programs they fund — including schools, which account for a huge portion of the state’s budget since the passage of Proposition 13, the 1978 measure that limited local governments’ ability to raise property taxes.
When revenues nosedive, lawmakers at all levels of government typically ask voters to approve tax increases at the ballot box — when they can least afford them.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
On the flip side, when the stock market is booming, California is constrained by the Gann Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416), an obscure rule that prevents the state from spending more per taxpayer than it did in 1979 — the year voters approved the measure — once adjusted for inflation. Any money the state collects over the limit must be refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as infrastructure or education.
In 2014, voters approved a ballot measure that stabilized this budget chaos. (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2014/prop-2-110414.aspx) It did three main things:
First, it required the state to set aside 1.5% of general fund tax revenue each year. Second, whenever the state collected especially high capital gains tax revenue, it required some of that money to be set aside. Third, it directed the state to put half the combined funds in a rainy-day savings account and use the other half to make additional payments on long-term retiree healthcare and pension debt through 2030.
These rules “substantially improved” (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) California’s reserve policy, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, permitting the state’s savings account to go from basically zilch to $23 billion.
But it wasn’t nearly sufficient to smooth out the state’s budget volatility.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The 2014 measure capped the rainy-day fund at 10% of the general fund — only enough to cover about one-third of likely shortfalls during the next 50 years, the Legislative Analyst’s Office concluded after running thousands of simulations.
To make up the difference, California would have to cut core services during every economic downturn or raise taxes.
Neither are good options.
Prop 2, which was inspired by the Legislative Analyst’s Office research, is designed to create conditions for a stabler budget.
The measure would double California’s reserve cap to 20% of general fund dollars and direct the state to save an even larger share of capital gains windfalls. It would also require California to keep making additional debt payments through 2040 and permit funds set aside for this purpose to be spent on a wider variety of debts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop2-110326.pdf), including repaying loans from the federal government and state special funds that backfilled holes in the general fund.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
These provisions aren’t particularly controversial. Even Republican Assembly Member David Tangipa of Fresno, a Prop 2 opponent, acknowledged to the editorial board that “I supported quite a bit of the measure.”
The sticking point for him and others who oppose Prop 2 centers on the Gann Limit.
Currently, depositing money into the rainy-day fund counts as “spending” under the Gann Limit. Ironically, this can discourage lawmakers from putting money into reserves in good budget years — which is precisely when they should be socking funds away.
Prop 2 would change that calculus by counting withdrawals from the account as spending under the Gann Limit — leaving lawmakers with fewer excuses for not filling the rainy-day fund during boom years.
Tangipa argued that this “takes away the ability to actually reimburse the taxpayers money that belongs to them.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But padding the rainy-day fund in flush budget years arguably saves taxpayers money in the long run by increasing stability and decreasing the likelihood of taxes in down years. The Legislative Analyst’s Office described the proposed accounting tweak as “reasonable.”
If used to the fullest extent, Prop 2 could improve California’s budget stability, permitting the state to cover about 50% of funding shortfalls in the next 50 years (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028).
That’s better than the 30% it can cover now. Still, Prop 2 is a far cry from the model the Legislative Analyst’s Office recommended: raising California’s reserve cap to 50% by 2055, either by establishing more robust deposit rules or setting aside much more capital gains tax revenue in especially flush years.
This framework, the analyst’s office found, would allow the state to absorb 75% of funding shortfalls in the next 50 years.
Lawmakers considered the 50% cap, but “we realized that was not going to be an achievable level, both politically and from a policy perspective,” Assembly Member Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino (Los Angeles County), and Prop 2’s author, told the editorial board.
Nevertheless, he said, Prop 2 is one of the most “concrete and achievable” things “we can do in the near term that would put California on stronger financial footing.”
The catch, Gabriel acknowledged: “You still need responsible decision-makers.”
In other words, Prop 2 is effectively useless if politicians don’t exercise fiscal prudence.
Prop 2’s deposit and withdrawal rules can be waived during a natural disaster or if the governor and Legislature declare a fiscal emergency — and the state’s criteria for one are farcical.
Case in point: California’s revenue is currently booming (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5187) amid an overheated stock market, but Gov. Gavin Newsom and the Legislature have declared multiple fiscal emergencies in recent years — postponing deposits into the rainy-day fund, pulling billions of dollars out of reserves and raising taxes on everyday Californians (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/tax-money-state-california-22325976.php) to maintain$100 billion in spending growth (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5176).

“There are natural political incentives to spend when you have a lot of money,” Gabriel admitted. Prop 2 won’t necessarily curb those, but if used appropriately, it could improve California’s budget resilience and make it harder for lawmakers to justify reckless spending during good years — and then beg voters for more money when the economy turns south.
Voters should pass Prop 2 and hold lawmakers accountable to their promise to be more responsible stewards of taxpayer money.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
Now I have a comprehensive view. Let me also quickly check the LA Times piece for the opposition perspective and maybe check whether the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association opposes it. Let me also check the LAO's report on the 50% reserve recommendation mentioned in the Chronicle endorsement, which supports the idea that larger reserves are prudent.

Summary of my research so far:

**Proposition 2 (Nov 3, 2026, California)** — "Save for California's Future Act" (ACA 20, Gabriel):
1. Doubles the rainy day fund (BSA) cap from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenues
2. Sets aside more (150%) of capital gains revenues above 10% of GF revenues during boom years
3. Extends the 50/50 split (reserve deposits / debt paydown) through 2039-40 instead of 2029-30
4. Expands eligible debt paydown: federal UI loans (~$20B), Prop 98 settle-up obligations, Medi-Cal loans, etc.
5. Changes Gann Limit accounting: deposits into BSA and the holding account don't count when deposited but count when withdrawn
6. Simplifies budget emergency declaration (May Revision can serve as proclamation)

**Supporters:** Gov. Newsom, legislative Democrats (+ some Republicans; passed 59-8 Assembly, 29-2 Senate), CA Professional Firefighters, LA Chamber of Commerce, CA Hospital Association, CA Primary Care Association, CA State PTA, education leaders, labor unions. Editorial endorsements: SF Chronicle (yes, with caveats), Sacramento Bee/McClatchy (yes), SPUR (yes), Bay Area Reporter (yes).

**Opponents:** Assemblymember David Tangipa (R, Fresno) — though he acknowledged to the Chronicle editorial board he "supported quite a bit of the measure"; Carl DeMaio/Reform California; Steven Choi; most Republican lawmakers. Main arguments: Gann Limit loophole making taxpayer rebates less likely; no new guaranteed funding; "slush fund" rhetoric; Legislators suspended $5B+ in deposits within 24 hours of placing measure on ballot.

**Key neutral/independent facts:**
- LAO (nonpartisan): 2014 rules "substantially improved" reserve policy, building the fund from ~zero to $23B; the 10% cap covers only ~1/3 of likely shortfalls over the next 50 years; LAO recommended even going to 50% by 2055 (which would cover 75% of shortfalls). LAO described the Gann Limit accounting tweak as "reasonable." LAO's ballot analysis says reserves would be higher and balancing the budget would be "somewhat easier when revenues decline."
- The state's revenue structure is extremely volatile (top 1% of earners pay ~50% of income taxes; capital gains dependent).
- The rainy day fund proved its worth during COVID and recent deficits ($12.2B drawn down over two years).
- The Gann Limit rebate provision has rarely ever been triggered (last time decades ago — 1987 was the only rebate); the state currently has $27B of headroom under the limit, so the change matters only in boom years when revenue surges.
- Even the leading legislative opponent (Tangipa) said he "supported quite a bit of the measure."
- The debt paydown extension (through 2040, including UI debt, Prop 98 obligations) is described by Hoover as "the most concrete and least disputed piece" that "most budget analysts across the spectrum tend to endorse."

**Counter-arguments for voting No:**
- Excluding deposits from the Gann Limit makes taxpayer rebates less likely — a loosening of a voter-approved constitutional guardrail (though money still counts when withdrawn)
- Opportunity cost: money locked away in reserves/debt isn't available for current services or tax relief
- The Legislature can still waive deposits during declared emergencies, so discipline isn't guaranteed (though the emergency withdrawal rules remain unchanged — only half can be withdrawn in the first year, and debt payments can't be suspended)
- CalBudgetCenter (left-leaning) has nuanced critiques: using set-asides to repay UI debt shifts business-borne costs to the state and doesn't fix the broken UI system; some boom-year revenue could otherwise fund critical needs
- Hypocrisy concern: legislators suspended deposits recently

**Weighing it:**
The core question: Is it better for California to have a bigger constitutionally-mandated reserve and continued debt paydown, accepting a change in Gann Limit accounting timing (and thus making rebates less likely)?

Arguments in favor of YES seem stronger to me:
1. The problem is real and well-documented: California's revenue volatility is extreme, and the current 10% cap is objectively insufficient per the nonpartisan LAO (covers only ~1/3 of likely shortfalls).
2. The 2014 rainy day fund demonstrably worked (COVID, recent deficits), and doubling the cap extends this proven mechanism.
3. The measure forces MORE saving in boom years rather than more spending — it constrains the Legislature's ability to spend windfalls on ongoing programs, which is the opposite of a "slush fund." Money in the BSA can only be withdrawn during declared budget emergencies, and only limited amounts (half in year one).
4. The debt paydown extension is broadly endorsed across the spectrum, including paying down the $20B federal UI loan and Prop 98 obligations to schools.
5. The Gann Limit change is mostly a timing clarification that removes a genuine disincentive to save; the LAO called it "reasonable." The money still counts against the limit when spent. The rebate provision has almost never been triggered in practice (once, in 1987), and the state currently has ~$27B of headroom.
6. Broad bipartisan legislative support (59-8, 29-2), broad coalition of supporters (firefighters, hospitals, PTA, chamber of commerce, educators).
7. Editorial boards across the spectrum recommend yes (Chronicle, Bee/McClatchy, SPUR, BAR).

The No side's arguments are mostly rhetorical ("slush fund," "cancels your tax rebate") and the rebate concern is somewhat speculative given the rebate mechanism's rarity. Even the lead legislative opponent conceded he supported most of the measure. The main legitimate concerns are (a) opportunity cost of savings vs. current spending — a values tradeoff that fiscal prudence generally favors given volatility; and (b) the Legislature's past willingness to suspend deposits — but Prop 2 preserves and even strengthens incentives to save (e.g., counting withdrawals against the Gann Limit means withdrawing in boom years would be costly; and debt payments still can't be suspended).

One more consideration: the CalBudgetCenter critique about UI debt shifting business costs to the state. That's a real critique from the left, but it's about how the state might use a tool, not about whether the tool should exist. Paying down the federal UI loan would save businesses from automatic federal tax increases and save the state from paying ~$1B/year in interest — arguably a reasonable use.

Also the Hoover analysis, which presents risks and benefits even-handedly, seems to lean toward acknowledging the measure addresses a real problem ("A bigger fund that fills faster in boom years is a direct answer to a real and repeated problem") while noting the debt paydown is "the part most budget analysts across the spectrum tend to endorse" and the reserve expansion is the contested part. Hoover doesn't make an explicit recommendation in what I read, but its analysis is balanced.

Let me do a couple more searches to see if there are any strong independent arguments against that I've missed — e.g., Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association position, and the CalMatters/other polling or result data (since this seems to be a live election in November 2026 — the CalMatters link mentioned "election day" results framing, but the guide is for Nov 3, 2026). Also let me check the LA Times article. Actually, I already have the LA Times summary from the search snippet: "Democrats want more spending flexibility from California voters... The measure, supported by Gov. Gavin Newsom, seeks to exempt deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit... could receive push back from taxpayer advocates."

Let me check whether the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association took a position, and look at the LAO's 50% recommendation report briefly. Also maybe check CalMatters' explainer.

Actually, I think I have enough to decide, but let me do one more round of searches for due diligence — particularly the HJTA position and any polling showing the state of the race (which might indicate the vote is close or not). Actually, polls aren't really relevant to how I should answer. But an important consideration: the user asks "Is it better to vote yes or no on this prop?" — I should give a single answer of yes or no, based on the merits.

Let me do a final check on HJTA and any other notable opposition (e.g., taxpayer groups) and any good critiques of the emergency-declaration simplification provision (the "May Revision as proclamation" change) — that could be a genuine concern about making it easier to tap the fund. Let me search for that.
I have a strong picture now. Let me do a final round of checks — the taxpayer groups' positions, the LA Times coverage, and the LAO's underlying research on reserve adequacy.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-dateline data-subscriber-content> SACRAMENTO — Democratic leaders of the California Legislature approved aconstitutional amendment Thursday for the November ballot that asks voters to give them more flexibility over state spending and allow them to save money that could otherwise go back to taxpayers.
The measure, supported by Gov. Gavin Newsom, seeks to exempt deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters adopted through a series of ballot measures dating back to the late 1970s and to increase the share of tax revenue that can be put into the rainy day fund.
“Putting money aside to protect ourselves from future uncertainties isn’t just good government; it’s common sense,” Newsom said in a statement. “California is strong and resilient, but we’re not immune to economic headwinds. At a time when our essential services are under pressure, we have a responsibility to safeguard the programs and investments that Californians rely on.”
Advertisement
Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, which Democrats are calling the “Save for California’s Future Act,” could receive push back from taxpayer advocates.
Under an existing state appropriations restraint, also known as the Gann Limit, lawmakers cannot spend more than an amount determined by a formula that takes annual tax proceeds, changes to the population and cost of living into consideration. Tax revenue above the limit must be divided between schools and refunds to taxpayers.
With few exceptions, the limit applies to most appropriations of tax revenue, including money that lawmakers tuck away into the rainy day fund and other reserves. California voters have also capped the amount of money lawmakers can set aside in the rainy day fund to 10% of general fund proceeds in a given year.
Advertisement
Since taking office, Newsom has argued that it doesn’t make sense for savings to count as spending under state law.
State budget revenue is subject to dramatic swings from year to year based on stock market activity. The law, Newsom has said, prevents the state from saving more money in good years to stave off cuts to programs in bad years.
The proposed changes would exempt deposits into the rainy day fund and a short term reserve, called the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, from the state appropriations limit. The cap on the rainy day fund would grow from 10% of general fund tax revenue to 20%.
“Californians live by a simple, bipartisan truth: set money aside when times are good so you’re ready when they’re not,” Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (D-Hollister) said in a statement. “The Save For California’s Future Act is what responsible leadership looks like — and future taxpayers will thank us for it.”
The measure could incentivize Democrats to save more money because funds tucked away in the rainy day fund would no longer be considered expenditures counted toward the spending limit. By allowing lawmakers to set aside more money that is not subjected to state spending limits, it could also allow them to hold onto money that would be returned to taxpayers under current law.
The measure was approved Thursday at the state Capitol. Voters will consider the proposal on the November ballot.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-dateline data-subscriber-content> SACRAMENTO — Democratic leaders of the California Legislature approved aconstitutional amendment Thursday for the November ballot that asks voters to give them more flexibility over state spending and allow them to save money that could otherwise go back to taxpayers.
The measure, supported by Gov. Gavin Newsom, seeks to exempt deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters adopted through a series of ballot measures dating back to the late 1970s and to increase the share of tax revenue that can be put into the rainy day fund.
“Putting money aside to protect ourselves from future uncertainties isn’t just good government; it’s common sense,” Newsom said in a statement. “California is strong and resilient, but we’re not immune to economic headwinds. At a time when our essential services are under pressure, we have a responsibility to safeguard the programs and investments that Californians rely on.”

Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, which Democrats are calling the “Save for California’s Future Act,” could receive push back from taxpayer advocates.
Under an existing state appropriations restraint, also known as the Gann Limit, lawmakers cannot spend more than an amount determined by a formula that takes annual tax proceeds, changes to the population and cost of living into consideration. Tax revenue above the limit must be divided between schools and refunds to taxpayers.
With few exceptions, the limit applies to most appropriations of tax revenue, including money that lawmakers tuck away into the rainy day fund and other reserves. California voters have also capped the amount of money lawmakers can set aside in the rainy day fund to 10% of general fund proceeds in a given year.
Advertisement
Since taking office, Newsom has argued that it doesn’t make sense for savings to count as spending under state law.
State budget revenue is subject to dramatic swings from year to year based on stock market activity. The law, Newsom has said, prevents the state from saving more money in good years to stave off cuts to programs in bad years.
The proposed changes would exempt deposits into the rainy day fund and a short term reserve, called the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, from the state appropriations limit. The cap on the rainy day fund would grow from 10% of general fund tax revenue to 20%.
“Californians live by a simple, bipartisan truth: set money aside when times are good so you’re ready when they’re not,” Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (D-Hollister) said in a statement. “The Save For California’s Future Act is what responsible leadership looks like — and future taxpayers will thank us for it.”
The measure could incentivize Democrats to save more money because funds tucked away in the rainy day fund would no longer be considered expenditures counted toward the spending limit. By allowing lawmakers to set aside more money that is not subjected to state spending limits, it could also allow them to hold onto money that would be returned to taxpayers under current law.
The measure was approved Thursday at the state Capitol. Voters will consider the proposal on the November ballot.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-dateline data-subscriber-content> SACRAMENTO — Democratic leaders of the California Legislature approved aconstitutional amendment Thursday for the November ballot that asks voters to give them more flexibility over state spending and allow them to save money that could otherwise go back to taxpayers.
The measure, supported by Gov. Gavin Newsom, seeks to exempt deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters adopted through a series of ballot measures dating back to the late 1970s and to increase the share of tax revenue that can be put into the rainy day fund.
“Putting money aside to protect ourselves from future uncertainties isn’t just good government; it’s common sense,” Newsom said in a statement. “California is strong and resilient, but we’re not immune to economic headwinds. At a time when our essential services are under pressure, we have a responsibility to safeguard the programs and investments that Californians rely on.”
Advertisement
Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, which Democrats are calling the “Save for California’s Future Act,” could receive push back from taxpayer advocates.
Under an existing state appropriations restraint, also known as the Gann Limit, lawmakers cannot spend more than an amount determined by a formula that takes annual tax proceeds, changes to the population and cost of living into consideration. Tax revenue above the limit must be divided between schools and refunds to taxpayers.
With few exceptions, the limit applies to most appropriations of tax revenue, including money that lawmakers tuck away into the rainy day fund and other reserves. California voters have also capped the amount of money lawmakers can set aside in the rainy day fund to 10% of general fund proceeds in a given year.
Advertisement
Since taking office, Newsom has argued that it doesn’t make sense for savings to count as spending under state law.
State budget revenue is subject to dramatic swings from year to year based on stock market activity. The law, Newsom has said, prevents the state from saving more money in good years to stave off cuts to programs in bad years.
The proposed changes would exempt deposits into the rainy day fund and a short term reserve, called the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, from the state appropriations limit. The cap on the rainy day fund would grow from 10% of general fund tax revenue to 20%.
“Californians live by a simple, bipartisan truth: set money aside when times are good so you’re ready when they’re not,” Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (D-Hollister) said in a statement. “The Save For California’s Future Act is what responsible leadership looks like — and future taxpayers will thank us for it.”
The measure could incentivize Democrats to save more money because funds tucked away in the rainy day fund would no longer be considered expenditures counted toward the spending limit. By allowing lawmakers to set aside more money that is not subjected to state spending limits, it could also allow them to hold onto money that would be returned to taxpayers under current law.
The measure was approved Thursday at the state Capitol. Voters will consider the proposal on the November ballot.

Now I have a comprehensive view. Let me also quickly check the LA Times piece for the opposition perspective and maybe check whether the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association opposes it. Let me also check the LAO's report on the 50% reserve recommendation mentioned in the Chronicle endorsement, which supports the idea that larger reserves are prudent.

Summary of my research so far:

**Proposition 2 (Nov 3, 2026, California)** — "Save for California's Future Act" (ACA 20, Gabriel):
1. Doubles the rainy day fund (BSA) cap from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenues
2. Sets aside more (150%) of capital gains revenues above 10% of GF revenues during boom years
3. Extends the 50/50 split (reserve deposits / debt paydown) through 2039-40 instead of 2029-30
4. Expands eligible debt paydown: federal UI loans (~$20B), Prop 98 settle-up obligations, Medi-Cal loans, etc.
5. Changes Gann Limit accounting: deposits into BSA and the holding account don't count when deposited but count when withdrawn
6. Simplifies budget emergency declaration (May Revision can serve as proclamation)

**Supporters:** Gov. Newsom, legislative Democrats (+ some Republicans; passed 59-8 Assembly, 29-2 Senate), CA Professional Firefighters, LA Chamber of Commerce, CA Hospital Association, CA Primary Care Association, CA State PTA, education leaders, labor unions. Editorial endorsements: SF Chronicle (yes, with caveats), Sacramento Bee/McClatchy (yes), SPUR (yes), Bay Area Reporter (yes).

**Opponents:** Assemblymember David Tangipa (R, Fresno) — though he acknowledged to the Chronicle editorial board he "supported quite a bit of the measure"; Carl DeMaio/Reform California; Steven Choi; most Republican lawmakers. Main arguments: Gann Limit loophole making taxpayer rebates less likely; no new guaranteed funding; "slush fund" rhetoric; Legislators suspended $5B+ in deposits within 24 hours of placing measure on ballot.

**Key neutral/independent facts:**
- LAO (nonpartisan): 2014 rules "substantially improved" reserve policy, building the fund from ~zero to $23B; the 10% cap covers only ~1/3 of likely shortfalls over the next 50 years; LAO recommended even going to 50% by 2055 (which would cover 75% of shortfalls). LAO described the Gann Limit accounting tweak as "reasonable." LAO's ballot analysis says reserves would be higher and balancing the budget would be "somewhat easier when revenues decline."
- The state's revenue structure is extremely volatile (top 1% of earners pay ~50% of income taxes; capital gains dependent).
- The rainy day fund proved its worth during COVID and recent deficits ($12.2B drawn down over two years).
- The Gann Limit rebate provision has rarely ever been triggered (last time decades ago — 1987 was the only rebate); the state currently has $27B of headroom under the limit, so the change matters only in boom years when revenue surges.
- Even the leading legislative opponent (Tangipa) said he "supported quite a bit of the measure."
- The debt paydown extension (through 2040, including UI debt, Prop 98 obligations) is described by Hoover as "the most concrete and least disputed piece" that "most budget analysts across the spectrum tend to endorse."

**Counter-arguments for voting No:**
- Excluding deposits from the Gann Limit makes taxpayer rebates less likely — a loosening of a voter-approved constitutional guardrail (though money still counts when withdrawn)
- Opportunity cost: money locked away in reserves/debt isn't available for current services or tax relief
- The Legislature can still waive deposits during declared emergencies, so discipline isn't guaranteed (though the emergency withdrawal rules remain unchanged — only half can be withdrawn in the first year, and debt payments can't be suspended)
- CalBudgetCenter (left-leaning) has nuanced critiques: using set-asides to repay UI debt shifts business-borne costs to the state and doesn't fix the broken UI system; some boom-year revenue could otherwise fund critical needs
- Hypocrisy concern: legislators suspended deposits recently

**Weighing it:**
The core question: Is it better for California to have a bigger constitutionally-mandated reserve and continued debt paydown, accepting a change in Gann Limit accounting timing (and thus making rebates less likely)?

Arguments in favor of YES seem stronger to me:
1. The problem is real and well-documented: California's revenue volatility is extreme, and the current 10% cap is objectively insufficient per the nonpartisan LAO (covers only ~1/3 of likely shortfalls).

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-dateline data-subscriber-content> SACRAMENTO — Democratic leaders of the California Legislature approved aconstitutional amendment Thursday for the November ballot that asks voters to give them more flexibility over state spending and allow them to save money that could otherwise go back to taxpayers.
The measure, supported by Gov. Gavin Newsom, seeks to exempt deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters adopted through a series of ballot measures dating back to the late 1970s and to increase the share of tax revenue that can be put into the rainy day fund.
“Putting money aside to protect ourselves from future uncertainties isn’t just good government; it’s common sense,” Newsom said in a statement. “California is strong and resilient, but we’re not immune to economic headwinds. At a time when our essential services are under pressure, we have a responsibility to safeguard the programs and investments that Californians rely on.”
Advertisement
Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20, which Democrats are calling the “Save for California’s Future Act,” could receive push back from taxpayer advocates.
Under an existing state appropriations restraint, also known as the Gann Limit, lawmakers cannot spend more than an amount determined by a formula that takes annual tax proceeds, changes to the population and cost of living into consideration. Tax revenue above the limit must be divided between schools and refunds to taxpayers.
With few exceptions, the limit applies to most appropriations of tax revenue, including money that lawmakers tuck away into the rainy day fund and other reserves. California voters have also capped the amount of money lawmakers can set aside in the rainy day fund to 10% of general fund proceeds in a given year.
Advertisement
Since taking office, Newsom has argued that it doesn’t make sense for savings to count as spending under state law.
State budget revenue is subject to dramatic swings from year to year based on stock market activity. The law, Newsom has said, prevents the state from saving more money in good years to stave off cuts to programs in bad years.
The proposed changes would exempt deposits into the rainy day fund and a short term reserve, called the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, from the state appropriations limit. The cap on the rainy day fund would grow from 10% of general fund tax revenue to 20%.
“Californians live by a simple, bipartisan truth: set money aside when times are good so you’re ready when they’re not,” Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (D-Hollister) said in a statement. “The Save For California’s Future Act is what responsible leadership looks like — and future taxpayers will thank us for it.”
The measure could incentivize Democrats to save more money because funds tucked away in the rainy day fund would no longer be considered expenditures counted toward the spending limit. By allowing lawmakers to set aside more money that is not subjected to state spending limits, it could also allow them to hold onto money that would be returned to taxpayers under current law.
The measure was approved Thursday at the state Capitol. Voters will consider the proposal on the November ballot.

Now I have a comprehensive view. Let me summarize the state of the debate:

**Proposition 2 (November 3, 2026, California ballot)** — "Save for California's Future Act" (ACA 20):

What it does:
1. Doubles the rainy day fund (BSA) cap from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenues
2. Requires larger set-asides in boom years (150% of capital gains revenue above 10% of GF revenues)
3. Extends the 50/50 reserve/debt-paydown split through 2039-40 (instead of 2029-30)
4. Expands eligible debt paydown: federal UI loans (~$20B), Prop 98 settle-up obligations, Medi-Cal loans
5. Changes Gann Limit accounting: deposits into BSA and holding account don't count when deposited but count when withdrawn
6. Simplifies budget emergency declaration (May Revision can serve as proclamation)

Supporters: Newsom, Democratic Party, LA Chamber, League of Women Voters, CA Professional Firefighters, CA Hospital Association, CA Primary Care Association, CA State PTA, labor unions, educators. Editorial endorsements: SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, SPUR, Bay Area Reporter, Berkeley Political Review. Passed legislature 59-8 (Assembly), 29-2 (Senate) — bipartisan.

Opponents: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, California Taxpayers Association, Reform California (Carl DeMaio), Assemblymember David Tangipa, most Republican lawmakers, Steven Choi.

Key neutral analysis:
- LAO: reserves would be higher; balancing the budget "somewhat easier when revenues decline." LAO found the 2014 rules "substantially improved" reserve policy (zero → $23B). LAO simulations: 10% cap covers only ~1/3 of likely shortfalls over 50 years; 20% cap would cover ~50%; LAO's recommended 50% cap would cover 75%. LAO called the Gann Limit timing tweak "reasonable."
- The Gann Limit rebate has been triggered rarely in history (the state has ~$27B headroom currently); rebates are unlikely regardless.
- Even leading legislative opponent Tangipa told the Chronicle editorial board he "supported quite a bit of the measure."
- The rainy day fund demonstrably worked during COVID and recent deficits ($12.2B drawn down over two years, averted drastic cuts).
- HJTA's opposition is more about what the measure does NOT do ("falls far short of real spending reform... a Band-Aid on a severed limb") while acknowledging the reserve treatment "makes sense from the perspective of addressing revenue volatility."

The case for YES:
- Addresses a real, documented problem (extreme revenue volatility; recent $50B deficits after $100B surpluses)
- Forces MORE saving, not spending, in boom years — takes money off the table from legislators
- Extends debt paydown (broadly supported across spectrum)
- LAO-inspired; LAO called the Gann tweak "reasonable"
- Broad bipartisan legislative support and diverse coalition
- Even critics concede most of the measure is sound
- The "slush fund" claim is largely rhetoric — BSA withdrawals are still limited to budget emergencies, half in the first year; debt payments can't be suspended

The case for NO:
- Gann Limit accounting change makes taxpayer rebates less likely (legitimate concern for those who value the Gann Limit's refund mechanism)
- Opportunity cost of savings vs. current spending/tax relief
- Legislature can still suspend deposits (discipline not guaranteed)
- HJTA: measure doesn't fix structural overspending

On balance, I find the case for YES stronger:
1. The core problem (volatility) is real and severe, and bigger reserves are the direct remedy, endorsed by the nonpartisan LAO's research.
2. The mechanism is proven — the 2014 fund worked exactly as designed in COVID and recent deficits.
3. The Gann Limit change is a timing fix that the LAO itself called "reasonable" — money still counts against the limit when spent; it just stops penalizing saving. The rebate scenario is rare and the state has substantial headroom.
4. The debt-paydown extension is the least controversial piece, endorsed across the spectrum.
5. The measure constrains legislative spending impulses in boom years (requires more savings) — the opposite of a "slush fund."
6. Nearly unanimous legislative support including some Republicans; no formal opposition submitted to the voter guide.

The main No arguments are largely rhetorical or based on a preference for the Gann Limit's refund mechanism over reserve-building, plus generalized distrust of the Legislature. While the distrust is not entirely unearned (deposits were suspended during recent deficits), that's an argument about implementation, not design — and even then, the fund performed its intended function.

I'll answer YES.

6. Simplifies budget emergency declaration (May Revision can serve as proclamation)

Supporters: Newsom, Democratic Party, LA Chamber, League of Women Voters, CA Professional Firefighters, CA Hospital Association, CA Primary Care Association, CA State PTA, labor unions, educators. Editorial endorsements: SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, SPUR, Bay Area Reporter, Berkeley Political Review. Passed legislature 59-8 (Assembly), 29-2 (Senate) — bipartisan.

Opponents: Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, California Taxpayers Association, Reform California (Carl DeMaio), Assemblymember David Tangipa, most Republican lawmakers, Steven Choi.

Key neutral analysis:
- LAO: reserves would be higher; balancing the budget "somewhat easier when revenues decline." LAO found the 2014 rules "substantially improved" reserve policy (zero → $23B). LAO simulations: 10% cap covers only ~1/3 of likely shortfalls over 50 years; 20% cap would cover ~50%; LAO's recommended 50% cap would cover 75%. LAO called the Gann Limit timing tweak "reasonable."
- The Gann Limit rebate has been triggered rarely in history (the state has ~$27B headroom currently); rebates are unlikely regardless.
- Even leading legislative opponent Tangipa told the Chronicle editorial board he "supported quite a bit of the measure."
- The rainy day fund demonstrably worked during COVID and recent deficits ($12.2B drawn down over two years, averted drastic cuts).
- HJTA's opposition is more about what the measure does NOT do ("falls far short of real spending reform... a Band-Aid on a severed limb") while acknowledging the reserve treatment "makes sense from the perspective of addressing revenue volatility."

The case for YES:
- Addresses a real, documented problem (extreme revenue volatility; recent $50B deficits after $100B surpluses)
- Forces MORE saving, not spending, in boom years — takes money off the table from legislators
- Extends debt paydown (broadly supported across spectrum)
- LAO-inspired; LAO called the Gann tweak "reasonable"
- Broad bipartisan legislative support and diverse coalition
- Even critics concede most of the measure is sound
- The "slush fund" claim is largely rhetoric — BSA withdrawals are still limited to budget emergencies, half in the first year; debt payments can't be suspended

The case for NO:
- Gann Limit accounting change makes taxpayer rebates less likely (legitimate concern for those who value the Gann Limit's refund mechanism)
- Opportunity cost of savings vs. current spending/tax relief
- Legislature can still suspend deposits (discipline not guaranteed)
- HJTA: measure doesn't fix structural overspending

On balance, I find the case for YES stronger:
1. The core problem (volatility) is real and severe, and bigger reserves are the direct remedy, endorsed by the nonpartisan LAO's research.
2. The mechanism is proven — the 2014 fund worked exactly as designed in COVID and recent deficits.
3. The Gann Limit change is a timing fix that the LAO itself called "reasonable" — money still counts against the limit when spent; it just stops penalizing saving. The rebate scenario is rare and the state has substantial headroom.
4. The debt-paydown extension is the least controversial piece, endorsed across the spectrum.
5. The measure constrains legislative spending impulses in boom years (requires more savings) — the opposite of a "slush fund."
6. Nearly unanimous legislative support including some Republicans; no formal opposition submitted to the voter guide.

The main No arguments are largely rhetorical or based on a preference for the Gann Limit's refund mechanism over reserve-building, plus generalized distrust of the Legislature. While the distrust is not entirely unearned (deposits were suspended during recent deficits), that's an argument about implementation, not design — and even then, the fund performed its intended function.

if two conditions were met:
First, the conditions required for a budget emergency (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-rainy-day-fund-and-other-budget-reserves-overview/#h-projected-surplus-temporary-holding-account-a-place-to-set-aside-anticipated-surplus-revenues:~:text=The%20required%20annual%20deposit%20may%20be%20reduced%20or%20suspended%20in%20the%20event%20of%20a%20%E2%80%9Cbudget%20emergency.) would have to exist.
Second, the May Revision would have to propose suspending or reducing a required transfer to the BSA or PSSSA and/or withdrawing funds from one or both of these reserves.
In other words, if voters approve Prop. 2, the governor would no longer have to issue a formal proclamation in order for a budget emergency to be operative.
What Would Proposition 2 Not Do?
While Prop. 2 would make a few changes to California’s rainy day fund as well as modestly revise how the Gann Limit works, the measure would largely leave the current rules in place. In addition, Prop. 2 would not touch the state’s constitutional funding requirement for TK-14 schools and community colleges, known as Prop. 98. For example, Prop. 2:
Maintains the requirement to set aside 1.5% of state General Fund tax revenues each year. Half of these revenues would continue to go into the rainy day fund (BSA), and the other half would continue to be used to pay down certain state debts.
Continues to allow state leaders to reduce or suspend deposits into the rainy day fund to address a budget emergency, and maintains the current definition of “emergency.” BSA deposits could continue to be reduced or suspended in the event of a budget emergency, which would continue to be defined as 1) a disaster or extreme peril or 2) insufficient General Fund revenues to meet a prior-year spending level.
Continues to limit the amount of money that may be withdrawn from the rainy day fund to address a budget emergency. State leaders could continue to withdraw only the amount needed to address a budget emergency, and no more than half of the funds could be taken out in the first year of an emergency.
Continues to prohibit state leaders from suspending debt payments to address a budget emergency. State leaders would continue to be prevented from reducing or canceling required debt payments, even if the state faced a disaster or a severe budget shortfall.
Does not make any changes to the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee for TK-14 education. Under the state Constitution, the state is required to set aside a portion of revenues for schools and community colleges each year based on various inputs and formulas. Prop. 2 does not make any changes to the formulas or inputs that determine the annual minimum guarantee calculation.
Maintains the current rules for California’s TK-14 education reserve. Prop. 2 does not change the rules governing the PSSSA, the state’s reserve for TK-12 schools and community colleges. For example, all of the conditions required to trigger a deposit into the PSSSA would remain intact. This includes strong capital gains-related income tax revenue, General Fund revenue growth that translates to strong growth in the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee, and no legislative suspension of the guarantee.
Leaves California’s arbitrary spending cap largely untouched. Other than modestly changing the relationship between two state reserves and the Gann Limit, Prop. 2 leaves in place the complex rules that structure California’s spending cap. This cap hinders state leaders’ ability (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/) to respond to the needs of Californians even as these needs have changed dramatically since the Gann Limit was created in 1979.
What Would Proposition 2 Mean for California?
This section explores the implications of several key provisions of Prop. 2, specifically:
Raising the rainy day fund cap to from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenues,
Setting aside more General Fund revenues during “boom” years,
Expanding the types of state debt that may be paid down with set-aside revenues, including unemployment insurance loans and certain TK-14 education obligations, and
Changing the relationship between two state reserves and the state spending cap (the Gann Limit).
This section also considers the implications of maintaining two current rainy day fund provisions that Prop. 2 would leave in place, specifically:
Continuing to prohibit state leaders from reducing or suspending required debt payments during a budget emergency, and
Maintaining the current definition of what qualifies as a budget emergency.
What Are the Implications of Raising the Rainy Day Fund (BSA) Cap to 20% of General Fund Tax Revenues?
Under Prop. 2, the maximum size of the rainy day fund would double, rising from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenues. With a higher cap, the rainy day fund would have the potential to grow substantially larger. This, in turn, would provide a larger “cushion” for the state budget, helping state leaders to better protect vital services when revenues drop during economic downturns and reducing the need for draconian spending cuts that harm Californians.
If the BSA balance were ever to reach the higher 20% cap, the annual General Fund revenues that would otherwise be deposited into the fund (“spillover” revenue) would instead be spent on infrastructure, as under current law. However, with a higher cap, the state would reach the BSA limit less frequently than is currently the case with a 10% cap. Consequently, over time there would be less spillover revenue available for infrastructure investments. On the other hand, the rainy day fund would likely hold a larger balance to help address a budget emergency.
Curious About Other Ballot Propositions?
Browse our collection of resources covering California’s statewide ballot measures to help you understand what’s at stake for California this November.
See More Resources (https://calbudgetcenter.org/issues/ballot-propositions/)
What Are the Implications of Setting Aside More Revenue in “Boom” Years?
Prop. 2 would require the state to set aside more revenue in years when capital gains revenues spike. This change would allow the state to build up the rainy day fund and pay down certain debts faster, reducing future General Fund cost pressures, while modestly curtailing General Fund revenue available for immediate spending needs.
If Prop 2’s “excess” capital gains provisions had been in place between 2010-11 and 2023-24, California would have had to set aside more General Fund revenue in six of those 14 years. This additional set-aside would have amounted to less than 1% or 2% of total General Fund revenue in each of those six years. Capital gains revenue is difficult to project. However, if a similar pattern held going forward, Prop. 2 could take hundreds of millions of dollars — or even more than $1 billion — in revenue “off the table” in some years. This would reduce resources available to address urgent needs that arise, but would also help to pay down additional state debt and further build reserves to address future emergencies.
Although “excess” capital gains revenue, by definition, is not a predictable and reliable revenue source and cannot be counted on to fund ongoing services, it could be reasonable to use it to temporarily meet critical needs. For example, the state could provide more funding for food banks in the wake of federal food assistance cuts, boost support for local governments to address homelessness, and pay child care providers before or at the time of service delivery (rather than after) — a change that would increase providers’ financial solvency.
In certain years, Prop. 2 would modestly reduce revenue that could otherwise be used to support vital services as communities across the state are reeling from deep federal cuts and mounting affordability pressures that are compounding long-standing unmet needs.
However, meaningfully addressing Californians’ needs requires significant and sustained new revenue — well beyond the relatively modest revenue that Prop. 2 would occasionally divert to reserves and debt payments. This underscores the need to reform California’s outdated tax base whether or not voters approve Prop. 2.
What Are the Implications of Expanding the Types of Debt That May Be Paid Down with Set-Aside Revenues?
The state Constitution requires a portion of General Fund revenues to be set aside each year for certain debt payments (unfunded pension and state retiree health liabilities). This requirement cannot be reduced or suspended even in a budget emergency — a provision that Prop. 2 would leave in place. In recent years, for example, roughly $1 billion to $2 billion in General Fund revenues each year remained “off the table” and were not available to support urgent spending needs.
Prop. 2 would broaden the allowable uses of set-aside revenues to include unemployment insurance (UI) debt. If policymakers were to use these debt-paydown funds to repay the principal on the state’s federal UI loans, then a cost currently borne by businesses would be shifted to the state .
Prop. 2 would also allow set-aside revenues to be used to pay down certain obligations related to TK-14 education and Medi-Cal that otherwise would be paid out of the General Fund. If policymakers were to use debt-paydown funds for these purposes, then General Fund revenue would be freed up for other purposes .
However, set-aside revenues are limited. If state leaders were to use more of these debt-paydown funds for the new purposes allowed by Prop. 2, then fewer (or no) funds would be available to reduce unfunded pension and state retiree health liabilities — costs that would eventually be borne by the General Fund.
What Are the Implications of Using Set-Aside Revenues to Repay Unemployment Insurance Loans?
Prop. 2 would allow state leaders to use set-aside revenues for “federal loans made to the Unemployment Fund.” California owes the federal government roughly $20 billion it borrowed to cover the cost of workers’ unemployment insurance (UI) benefits beginning during the COVID-19 pandemic, when unemployment spiked. Using debt-paydown funds to reduce the principal on California’s UI debt would shift a cost currently borne by businesses to the state and do nothing to fix California’s broken UI system.
Shifting a Cost Currently Borne by Businesses to the State
California’s state government is not required to repay the principal on federal UI loans. Instead, federal law requires businesses to repay the principal through automatic increases in their federal payroll taxes. This makes sense: California’s UI debt is the result of a broken system (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/revitalizing-unemployment-insurance-in-california/). For decades, state leaders have not required businesses to contribute enough to cover the true cost of the unemployment benefits their workers need.
Using set-aside revenues to repay the principal on California’s UI loans would shift a cost currently covered by businesses to the state. Moreover, this approach would reduce the amount of debt-paydown funds available for other purposes, such as reducing unfunded pension liabilities — costs that would eventually be borne by the General Fund. As a result, to the extent that state leaders were to use set-aside revenues to pay down UI debt, then more General Fund revenue would be needed to reduce other state debts, diverting dollars away from providing services to Californians.
Doing Nothing to Fix California’s Broken UI System
The UI system is chronically underfunded (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/revitalizing-unemployment-insurance-in-california/) because California has failed to modernize the system’s financing to ensure that it generates sufficient revenue to cover the cost of the unemployment benefits workers need.
Consequently, federal loans are expected to become “a permanent feature (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4943)” of the program, with significant implications for the state’s budget. California typically uses General Fund dollars to pay the interest on these loans, which could total around $1 billion annually in the coming years. Using state dollars to pay the interest on UI loans reduces resources that could otherwise be used to address Californians’ affordability challenges or other needs.
Using debt-paydown funds to reduce the principal on California’s UI debt could modestly reduce the state’s annual interest payments in the near term. However, until state leaders address the broken UI financing system, California is expected to remain locked in a perpetual cycle of debt, necessitating ongoing federal loans and putting constant pressure on the state’s General Fund to cover the annual interest owed.
What Are the Implications of Using Set-Aside Revenues to Repay Certain School and Community College (TK-14) Education Obligations?
Prop. 2 would give state leaders a new option to use set-aside revenues to repay certain TK-14 education obligations. Specifically, the measure would allow state leaders to use these funds to 1) cover Prop. 98 “settle up” payments (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5110#Settle_Up), as needed, and 2) more quickly phase out an outstanding debt tied to an accounting maneuver that state leaders adopted in the 2023-24 budget (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4929) to address an issue related to the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. These new options mean that:
State Leaders Could Use Debt-Paydown Funds to Help Address Increases in Prop. 98 Funding Estimates
When state leaders enact a budget, they provide an estimate of the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee for that fiscal year. This initial estimate is updated in subsequent years to reflect changes in revenue estimates and other inputs. The updated inputs sometimes increase the Prop. 98 guarantee, which requires the state to provide additional funding through “settle-up” payments.
The state usually recognizes any increases to the Prop. 98 guarantee in subsequent years and provides the required settle-up payments from the state’s General Fund at that point. In some years, however, settle-up payments have been delayed, most recently for fiscal years 2024-25 and 2025-26, partly due to the state’s limited General Fund capacity to fund that growth.
Prop. 2 would allow set-aside revenues to be used to cover any current or future Prop. 98 settle-up obligations. This change would provide state leaders with an additional funding source for making these payments, which they could use at their discretion, potentially in combination with General Fund dollars. However, using debt-paydown funds for this purpose would compete with other allowable uses, such as prefunding state retiree health benefits.
In addition, using debt-paydown funds to make settle-up payments would not necessarily retire this obligation more quickly. Under current law, there is no required schedule for making settle-up payments, and Prop. 2 does not create one. If set-aside revenues were treated as the sole or primary source for settle-up payments, it could take longer to fully pay down these obligations because the amount of set-aside revenues may not align with the size of the obligation in a given year, especially when state revenues decline and the set-aside shrinks.
State Leaders Could Accelerate the State’s Recognition of $6.2 Billion in TK-14 Costs Incurred in 2022-23
In 2023, tax filing deadlines were extended due to winter storms, and state leaders overestimated the amount of tax revenue that would be received later in the year. As a result, the state provided $6.2 billion more to schools and community colleges than the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee actually required.
State leaders did not reduce the minimum guarantee to account for the lower revenues. Instead, they set up a schedule to recognize those dollars for accounting purposes in future budgets, starting in 2027-28 and ending in 2039-40. The annual cost is $500 million for the first 12 years, with a smaller amount in the 13th year.
Recognizing these costs will directly reduce General Fund revenues that would otherwise be available in those years for state funding priorities outside of the Prop. 98 guarantee. The sooner this $6.2 billion debt is recognized, the sooner the annual General Fund cost ends and those dollars become available for other purposes.
Prop. 2 would allow state leaders to use set-aside revenues to recognize this $6.2 billion debt, which would mitigate the General Fund impact as well as potentially clear the outstanding balance more quickly. However, using debt-paydown funds for this purpose would compete with other allowable uses, such as reducing state retiree pension liabilities.
What Are the Implications of Changing the Relationship Between Reserves and the State Spending Cap (Gann Limit)?
Prop. 2 would allow state policymakers to save more in strong revenue years to better protect vital public services during economic downturns. This is because deposits into two key reserves would no longer count as spending for the purpose of calculations required by California’s spending cap (the Gann Limit). Instead, these deposits would count toward the Gann Limit only when they are withdrawn .
This change would allow state leaders to build up reserves in years when revenues are strong and the state is close to reaching the spending cap, removing a key drawback of the Gann Limit. This change would also modestly increase “room” under the cap by up to a few billion dollars a year, potentially delaying how long it takes for the state to surpass the limit.
These changes are important. The Gann Limit is an arbitrary cap that hinders state leaders’ ability (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/) to respond to the needs of Californians, which have changed dramatically since late 1970s when the cap was established. Meeting the essential needs of residents and building up reserves to address future needs should not be hamstrung by an arbitrary spending cap approved by an earlier generation of voters.
Prop. 2 would allow policymakers to keep the state under the Gann Limit by making deposits into two reserves — the BSA and the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account (“holding account” (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-rainy-day-fund-and-other-budget-reserves-overview/)). Several factors, including which of these accounts were used for this purpose, would determine when the deposited funds could be withdrawn and how they could be spent. Specifically:
For deposits into the holding account , state law currently requires the funds to be withdrawn within a year — a rule that could be changed by the Legislature.
If withdrawing funds from the holding account would cause the state to exceed the spending cap, then policymakers would lose flexibility over how the funds could be used (their use would be governed by the Gann Limit’s restrictive rules (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/)).
Otherwise, if withdrawing the funds would not cause the state to exceed the limit, policymakers would have full control over the funds.
For deposits into the BSA , the portion that was constitutionally required to be deposited could not be withdrawn unless a budget emergency was operative. Any discretionary deposits, on the other hand, could be withdrawn at any time.
If withdrawing funds from the BSA would cause the state to exceed the spending limit, then policymakers would lose flexibility over how the funds could be used (their use would be governed by the Gann Limit’s restrictive rules (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/)).
